17	  after, headed `# m-<tid> <title>`, each of its lines an `m-<tid>-<num>`, so `rg -w m-<tid>`
18	  returns the whole thread. The directory is the thread's state, and any member may write a line
19	  in any open thread.
20	- **Thread id**: `<tid>`, an integer, never reused.
21	  - Its store is the tracked file `threads`, one integer, the last id issued, never decreased.
22	  - The opener reads it, adds one, writes it back, and takes the new value, in the opening commit.
23	- **Title**: the opener's, a few words, never changed.
24	- **Line**: one message or mark, one physical line, always, appended oldest first directly
25	  under the heading, no blank line anywhere in the file:
26	  `- m-<tid>-<num> <time> from <author> <action> <info>`.
27	- **Number**: `<num>`, an integer from 0, one more than the last line in the file, so the thread
28	  is its own counter and nothing else stores it: line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, and
29	  the next number is the file's line count less one. Every `m-<tid>-<num>` is unique and the numbers
30	  order the thread, so a search for one returns the line and every later line that names it. An
31	  id, thread or line, is final once written, since one clone mints them (see What is not here),
32	  and a rejected push, which only a second clone causes, renumbers before pushing again.
33	- **Time**: when the line was written, UTC to the second, `2026-09-09T16:05:42Z`. For a human
34	  reading the thread, never for ordering, as clocks may not agree.
35	- **Author**: the member who wrote the line, after the word `from`, which is there for the human
36	  eye, since the position already says it.
37	- **Action**: what the line does, one of two:
38	  - **`to`**: a message. Info is the recipients, comma-joined with no spaces, a space, then the
39	    text. A recipient need not have been in the thread before, so a forward is a `to` naming the
40	    new member and saying what is forwarded. A reply begins its text with the id it answers when
41	    position alone would leave that ambiguous, as in a thread of three.
42	  - **`done`**: a mark, no info. The author has nothing to say to the lines before it. Any line
43	    from a member clears what was pending for them, so this is the line for when there is
44	    nothing else to write, and the closer's last word.
45	- **Info**: the message text, or its title and a message-link to its body,
46	  `[<title>](m-<tid>-<num>.md)`, relative to the thread's own directory so the link survives
47	  the close.
48	- **Body**: `m-<tid>-<num>.md` beside its thread, for a message that wants more than a line. It
49	  begins `# m-<tid>-<num> <title>`, so a search for the id finds it and the heading is an anchor,
50	  and it ends at the end of the file. Full markdown inside, headings, lists, and code blocks, and
51	  a quoted line is inert since a body is never read for lines. Moved with its thread.
52	- **Addressed**: a member is addressed by every `to` line naming them in its recipient field,
53	  and by nothing else. A member named in a line's text or in a body is referenced, never
54	  addressed, so a tool computing pending reads the recipient field, not the whole line.
55	- **Pending**: for a member, every `to` line naming them numbered above their latest line in
56	  that thread, of either action, all of them when they have written none. Their open
57	  obligations, and what Read messages returns: a line stays pending until they write after it,
58	  however many times it has been read, and a later line naming them makes them pending again.
59	  So a reply is its author's own clearance, and a question back puts the ball in the other
60	  court until the answer comes.
61	- **Complete**: every addressed member has a line numbered above every `to` line naming them.
62	  Computed from the file alone.
63	- **Closed**: the file is under `closed/`, moved there whole with its bodies, so every thread
64	  ever is in the tree, in this file's shape, and a reader parses one shape. History is
65	  provenance, never a store. A closed thread takes no line, and a late thought opens a new
66	  thread naming the old id.
67	- **Message-link**: a live link within this repo, `[<text>](<file>#<slug>)`, relative to the
68	  linking file and resolving to whatever the reader's checkout holds. The form for a body.
69	- **Sha-link**: a URL naming a commit SHA (`blob/<sha>/<path>#<slug>`), never a branch, which
70	  moves or dies. The form for content in another repo, where only a commit is durable.
71	- **Clone**: one, on one machine, one owner at a time, since the ids are allocated under its
72	  mutex (see What is not here). `owner` (gitignored) holds `<time> take|release <member>` lines,
73	  the time in a line's form, UTC to the second, and the last line names the owner. It is not a
74	  dotfile, so an `ls` shows who holds the clone.
75	- **Take ownership**: append a `take` line to `owner`. Yours until released. A `take` with no
76	  `release` after it means a session is writing, or died writing, and only a human tells the two
77	  apart and clears the second by writing the release.
78	- **Release ownership**: rewrite `owner` to the one `release` line, so the file holds at most
79	  the last release and the current take, and never grows. The clone is free.
80	
81	## Read Actions
82	
83	### Read messages
84	
85	This is a read only action, no ownership and no fetch.
86	
87	1. For each thread file, `open/m-<tid>.md` and never a body `open/m-<tid>-<num>.md`, find the
88	   `to` lines naming you. One numbered above your latest line in that file is pending, and the
89	   thread is the context to read it in.
90	2. Nothing pending, and `owner` shows no owner: consider doing a Fetch.
91	
92	A tool may do the search. The rule is the file, and the tool is a convenience.
93	
94	### Find a thread
95	
96	Every thread is in the tree, under `open/` or `closed/`.
97	
98	- Titles: `head -1 open/*.md closed/*.md`. Titles and openers: `head -2`.
99	- One thread: `cat open/m-<tid>.md` or `cat closed/m-<tid>.md`, `rg -w m-<tid>` for both and
100	  its bodies.
101	- A thread's commits, each titled with the thread ids it touched:
102	  `git log --oneline -- open/m-<tid>.md closed/m-<tid>.md`.
103	
104	## Write Actions
105	
106	Every write runs inside these guards, in order:
107	
108	- `Read messages` first, so the write answers the traffic as it stands.
109	- Read `owner`: no other member has taken ownership.
110	- Any guard failing: show the user and ask how to proceed.
111	- Re-read `owner` before releasing, and a `take` after yours means stop and show both lines.
112	- A rejected push: work with the user to correct the situation.
113	
114	Every write is an append: a thread file grows at its end, a body is a new file, and `threads` is
115	the one value that is overwritten. Nothing edits a line or a body once written.
116	
117	1. Take ownership.
118	2. Do any number of the actions below, in any threads: open, write lines, close. Each line
119	   follows its own rule, and the mutex serializes the write, not the action.
120	3. Release ownership. A commit is optional for lines: the mutex serializes the writers and a
121	   line carries its author and time, so an uncommitted line is as visible and as final as a
122	   pushed one, and the working copy may hold lines from several takes. Who commits is the
123	   humans' call, the member closing a thread the default, and the commit takes the working copy
124	   whole, titled with the ids of the threads it touches, ascending, `m-3 m-4`, whatever it does
125	   in them, lines, bodies, or a close, since the diff says which and the title is a convenience,
126	   never a store. Push when connected, since the remote is the copy no session can lose and the
127	   target every sha-link needs. A version commit is never optional (see Versions).
128	
129	### Fetch
130	
131	1. Ask the user, unless their permission is standing.
132	2. `git fetch`, or `jj git fetch --ignore-working-copy`, since a bare jj command snapshots the
133	   working copy, and that is a write.
134	
135	### Open a thread
136	
137	1. Read `threads`, add one, write it back. That is the thread id.
138	2. Create `open/m-<tid>.md`: the heading and the opener's `to` line, numbered 0, with its body
139	   file when it has one.
140	
141	### Write a line
142	
143	Follows Read messages. A reply, a forward, or a `done`, each a line, and each clears its
144	author's pending on its own. A reply answers everything the lines it clears asked, naming each
145	by id, accepted or not, and what it does not accept is said to the asker, so they are pending
146	again and the exchange runs until both agree or the humans settle it. What a message asks for
147	is done in the author's own project's records, a Todo or a cycle, which outlive the thread, and
148	the reply links the outcome by sha-link.
149	
150	1. The thread file exists under `open/`. One under `closed/` takes no line.
151	2. Append the line, numbered one more than the last line in the file, with its body file when
152	   it has one.
153	
154	### Close a thread
155	
156	The opener's to do, or any addressed member's when the opener has gone quiet, once the thread
157	is complete. The closer's `done`, when the last line names the closer, is what completes it,
158	and the close sits in the same commit.
159	
160	1. Move `open/m-<tid>.md` and its bodies, `open/m-<tid>-*.md`, to `closed/`.
161	
162	## What is not here
163	
164	- No inbox file. What is pending for a member is a query over `open/`, so a lost or stale inbox
165	  cannot disagree with the threads.
166	- No counter file per thread. The next number is read from the thread itself.
167	- No format version in the lines. The README's version is the rules', fields are additive,
168	  and a reader takes what is there.
169	- No second machine. The thread ids and line numbers are allocated under one clone's mutex, so
170	  two clones can mint the same id, a thread's from `threads` or a line's from the same last line.
171	  The rejected push catches it and the loser renumbers, which is why an id is final only once
172	  pushed. A second clone that never collides means member-scoped ids for threads and lines both,
173	  and that is the change it would take.
174	- No access control. Any member can modify or delete any file here. It works among friendly
175	  participants, and history is the only recourse.
176	- No commit per line. Under one clone the mutex is what keeps writes from interleaving, and a
177	  line's author and time are in the line, so a commit adds only the link to the session that
178	  wrote it. Committing batches lines, pushing backs them up, and the version commit is the one
179	  commit the rules require.
180	- No archive. `closed/` grows by a file per thread and its bodies, and git and `rg` carry that
181	  far past this family's traffic. The technique comes when it matters, a directory per year or a
182	  store outside the tree, and the ids, never reused, survive either.
183	
184	## Versions
185	
186	The title carries the rules' version, and the tree is always at that version: the commit that
187	bumps it edits this file and rewrites `open/` and `closed/` to the new shape in the same commit,
188	under the mutex, with every member's last push already in `main@origin`. History is never
189	rewritten, so a reader supports one shape, the one this file describes, and a tool that finds
190	the title behind it says so rather than parsing the past.
191	
192	- v0.3.3: a commit is titled with the ids of the threads it touches, `m-3 m-4`, a close
193	  included, so the close form and the line-id form go. The first batch under v0.3.2 carried five
194	  lines across two threads and five ids read as noise, and a commit that closed two threads had
195	  no title form, iiac-perf's finding at `m-3-1`. The title is a convenience, never a store, and
196	  the diff says what the commit did in each thread.
197	- v0.3.2: a commit that closes a thread is titled `close m-<tid> <title>` whatever lines it
198	  carries, and a title that lists ids is for a batch that closes nothing. The first close under
199	  v0.3.1, `13a7d9f7`, carried six lines, and six ids read as noise where the close is the event.
200	- v0.3.1: no blank line under the heading, so line `<num>` is file line `<num>` plus two, closed
201	  threads move to `closed/` instead of being deleted, a commit may carry any number of actions,
202	  the close in the same commit as its last `done`, and a release may leave lines uncommitted, so
203	  the clean-working-copy guard is gone and a commit batches whatever the working copy holds. A
204	  member's own line, of either action, clears what was pending for them, so a reply needs no
205	  `done` after it, `done` is the empty reply, and `read` is retired, since a line that clears
206	  nothing has no place in a query over lines. From the `m-2` replies: addressed means the
207	  recipient field alone, a reply answers everything it clears, naming each, and `owner`'s times
208	  are UTC to the second. The migration restored `m-1` from history without its blank line, its
209	  surplus `done` marks still valid lines.
210	- v0.3.0, the cutover from v0.2.0's records and inboxes: every record was complete, so no
211	  thread carried over. `threads` was created at 0, `notices.md`, `topics/`, the inboxes,
212	  `README-old.md`, and the `.owner` copy of the mutex were deleted, and the draft became this
213	  file. The v0.2.0 tree is the tag `v0.2.0`, and `git log -S'<heading>'` finds a record.
214

Today, my goal is to formally release v0.3.1 so I can start on using io_uring testing so we can use
our messaging system to issue linux operations to the kernel.

I've created `../TODO.md.vc-x1` where I've re-ordered the todo's of ./TODO.md, we need to verify it
"drop" any, I renamed and simplified:

### agent-files(proposal): a cycle is made by its own build

to:

### A cycle should dogfood it's own changes continuously

Also last cycle we tested a new technique which used `commit --local --scope work --no-push` to commit rungs. This
gives more flexibility to the user to explore the solution space. Historically we've tended to use a model
where each rung was `commit --scope both --push`. This is nice in that it guarantees that the agent-repo and
work-repo are both linear and synchronized. So last cycle we have a single commit on the agent-repo and
12 on the work-repo. I believe the work-repo is linear, I'd like us to verify that.

After looking at the linearity, the first Todo this cycle is an anomaly we ran into when closing. I want
to the user to be able to close a cycle to their liking and have it be obvious and for vc-x1 to help them
close it "properly". The basic operations are:
- close
- land
- push

And before or after any of those the user can "test" which may include:
- running "validate" using that any profile
- installing using any profile using that profile."<name>".suffix.

Actually, just thought of a new sub-command `init --local-test-repo <path>` and then be able use that test-repo as the
default repo all profiles, so maybe add [repos].test?

So let's discuss what to do next.

### agent-files(proposal): a cycle is made by its own build

(wink + agent, 2026-10-26) A cycle's rungs are committed by the installed `vc-x1`, which has none
of the cycle's code, so a change to `commit`, `push`, or `land` is tested by its unit tests alone
until it lands. **feat: vc-x1 land** found it at its closing, every rung made by `0.85.9`.

- A rung is committed by the cycle's build, the dev build installed after the rung before.
- The closing is made by a bootstrap, the release build of the working copy off the PATH, and the
  Land by the candidate, the committed closing's release build off the PATH, which then installs
  itself, `cmp` showing the binary tested is the one installed.
- The rules' Land and Close-out name the sequence, beside the README's `land` section.

### agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1

(wink + agent, 2026-10-29) `land`'s `--source` defaults to "the one local bookmark besides
`--onto`", which depends on every bookmark in the repo and fails once there are two. The rest of

- `--source` left out is `@-`, with the work `@` empty: what lands is then the tree validation ran

- The empty check is the work-repo's alone: the agent `@` holds the session and is never empty.
- An explicit `--source` lands what it names, with no check of `@`.
- The cycle's bookmark is found from `@-` as today: its own, else its nearest parent's above
  `--onto`, several refused with the list.
- The help: `--source <BM|REV>`, "The cycle's last commit, a bookmark or a revision [default: @-,

149	### install has a role and a profile
150	
151	(wink + agent, 2026-10-30) `[profile.dev]` holds both how a binary is built and what it is installed
152	as, so `vc-x1-dev` reads as the `dev` profile. Wink's model: they are two choices. The profile is how
153	it is compiled, `target/<profile>/<name>`, the name from `Cargo.toml`. The role is what it is: bare
154	`vc-x1` the released version and `vc-x1-dev` the development version, either from any profile.
155	`build` and `run` take a profile alone, and `install` alone has a role. Historically the install was
156	`cargo install --path . --locked`, sometimes with `--root` and a copy, before profiles existed.
157	
158	A proposal, the agent's, wink's to try (2026-10-30):
159	
160	- `[role.released]`, `default-profile = "release"`, and `[role.development]`, `suffix = "-dev"` and
161	  `default-profile = "dev"`. `suffix` leaves `[profile.*]`, and `[install] commands` says
162	  `{role.suffix}`.
163	- `install --as released|development`, the default the running binary's role by its name, so
164	  `vc-x1-dev install` stays development, and `--profile` overrides the role's default.
165	- A released install refuses a dirty build, a commit not on `main`, and a suffixed version unless
166	  `--force`, where today it only reports them. A development install reports them.
167	- The copy stays configured: `[install] commands` holds `cp {profile.bin}` and `mv`, or a project may
168	  list `cargo install --path . --locked --profile {profile.cargo} --root <dir>` and copy from
169	  `<dir>/bin`, which needs no path rule and, by cargo's help, shares the workspace's target directory.
170	  `bin` stays either way, since `run` needs it and `[build] commands` is not cargo-specific.
171	- A config with `suffix` under a profile is refused naming the move, or read as the role's for a
172	  while. Open.
173	
174	### desc takes a title, body, and trailers
175	
176	(wink + agent, 2026-10-30) Overwriting a commit's description takes three commands and leaves gaps:
177	`squash --title --body` on `@-` alone, needing both and folding `@`, `fix-desc --title` with no body
178	and only on a commit whose `ochid:` has an issue, and a hand-run `jj describe` for a trailer or a title. Wink's: `vc-x1 desc` gains optional `--title`, `--body`,
179	`--ochid`, and `--ocid`, in any combination, what is left out kept. With none it reads as it does
180	today. The agent's, to be agreed:
181	
182	- A write requires `-r`, one commit in one repo, so a default of `@` or a range writes nothing by
183	  accident, and `-s both` is refused, each repo's trailers being its own.
184	- `--ochid` repeats and replaces every `ochid:` line, since a Land's agent commit carries several, and

### install has a role and a profile

(wink + agent, 2026-10-30) `[profile.dev]` holds both how a binary is built and what it is installed
as, so `vc-x1-dev` reads as the `dev` profile. Wink's model: they are two choices. The profile is how
it is compiled, `target/<profile>/<name>`, the name from `Cargo.toml`. The role is what it is: bare
`vc-x1` the released version and `vc-x1-dev` the development version, either from any profile.
`build` and `run` take a profile alone, and `install` alone has a role. Historically the install was
`cargo install --path . --locked`, sometimes with `--root` and a copy, before profiles existed.

A proposal, the agent's, wink's to try (2026-10-30):

- `[role.released]`, `default-profile = "release"`, and `[role.development]`, `suffix = "-dev"` and
  `default-profile = "dev"`. `suffix` leaves `[profile.*]`, and `[install] commands` says
  `{role.suffix}`.
- `install --as released|development`, the default the running binary's role by its name, so
  `vc-x1-dev install` stays development, and `--profile` overrides the role's default.
- A released install refuses a dirty build, a commit not on `main`, and a suffixed version unless
  `--force`, where today it only reports them. A development install reports them.
- The copy stays configured: `[install] commands` holds `cp {profile.bin}` and `mv`, or a project may
  list `cargo install --path . --locked --profile {profile.cargo} --root <dir>` and copy from
  `<dir>/bin`, which needs no path rule and, by cargo's help, shares the workspace's target directory.
  `bin` stays either way, since `run` needs it and `[build] commands` is not cargo-specific.
- A config with `suffix` under a profile is refused naming the move, or read as the role's for a
  while. Open.

### desc takes a title, body, and trailers

(wink + agent, 2026-10-30) Overwriting a commit's description takes three commands and leaves gaps:
`squash --title --body` on `@-` alone, needing both and folding `@`, `fix-desc --title` with no body
and only on a commit whose `ochid:` has an issue, and a hand-run `jj describe` for a trailer or a title. Wink's: `vc-x1 desc` gains optional `--title`, `--body`,
`--ochid`, and `--ocid`, in any combination, what is left out kept. With none it reads as it does
today. The agent's, to be agreed:

- A write requires `-r`, one commit in one repo, so a default of `@` or a range writes nothing by
  accident, and `-s both` is refused, each repo's trailers being its own.
- `--ochid` repeats and replaces every `ochid:` line, since a Land's agent commit carries several, and
  `--ocid ""` removes the line.
- Only the description changes, nothing folds, and the tree is checked unchanged.
- A published commit is refused unless `--yes`, and `--dry-run` prints the result.
- `squash --title --body` and `fix-desc --title` then retire, and `commit -r`'s refusal names `desc`.

### init defaults to --local

(wink, 2026-10-30) `vc-x1 init` makes the workspace on the machine and creates and publishes nothing
unless `--push` asks, as `commit` does in **Only push publishes**. Today it creates the remotes and
pushes, public on GitHub unless `--private`, so a bare `init` publishes a repo.

- `--push` is what creates the remotes and publishes, and the approval it needs is the rest of that
  section's. `--private` and `--push-retries` take effect with it.
- Publishing later needs a way: a workspace with no `origin` has nothing for `vc-x1 push` to push to,
  so `push`, or a command of its own, creates the remotes.
- The trailers: `init`'s cross-links then have no URL to stamp, so they take the path form **feat:
  ochid trailers are URLs** defines, `/.agent-session/<chid>`, and they stay valid after a remote
  appears, the URL being checked only on a URL form.
- The name: `--repo local` is already a category, a local directory of bare repos, which is a remote
  of a kind and not this `--local`, so one of the two is renamed or explained. `clone` is to be
  checked for the same default.

vc-x1 0.85.18+4a827490b131

Land a cycle whose last commit is already made, on the machine: the
agent `@` committed when the cycle's commits name it, the links they
carry updated, --onto fast-forwarded to --source, and the cycle's
bookmark deleted, every check made before anything moves. --push also
publishes it, the agent repo first, and deletes the bookmark on
`origin`. `commit --closing ... --land` lands the same way, the
closing made first.

--source is a bookmark, the cycle's, or a revision, whose current
bookmark, else its nearest parent's above --onto, is the cycle's,
several refused with the list. Left out, it is the one local
bookmark besides --onto. --onto is a local bookmark at its
`origin` position that --source descends from, so a bushy tree lands
anywhere, and Land only fast-forwards: a merge is `commit
--closing`'s. --skip keeps a side of the cycle's bookmark, `local`,
`remote`, or `both`, and --delete-intermediate-bookmarks deletes the
bookmarks strictly between --onto and --source too. --dry-run makes
every check and says each step.

-s is required: `b` a dual workspace, the agent `main` moved with
the trunk, and `p` a plain repo. `w` alone could publish
trailers naming agent commits not yet published, and `a` alone has
no cycle to land, so both are refused. The install stays `vc-x1
install`, after.

positional is refused, naming -r.

--land's or `[cycle] trunk`, `main` when absent: one commit above the
trunk is finalized in place, more get the closing commit, the merge of
the trunk and the tip. A tip that is not @- is closed by a detour, @
moving onto it and returning after. --land [TRUNK] lands it: the trunk

check first: the one named, or for a revision the current or nearest
parent bookmark above the trunk, several refused with the list.

the agent half left to push, `a` the agent repo alone, unpaired, with
no trailer, and `p` a plain repo with no trailer. -R is optional and
says where. --body is the text, or @PATH to read it from a file.

          trunk and the tip

          dead-end closing", always on a closing commit

          Make the work commit the cycle's opening: " opening" is appended to

          Leave the line's bookmark where it is, rather than advancing it to the

          Publish what was committed, a commit otherwise staying on the machine

          Keep it on the machine, the default, saying so: nothing is pushed,
          `--opening`'s bookmark included
          
          [alias: --no-push]

          Stamp the `ochid:` alone, with no `ocid:` or `pcid:` links. `-s p` and
          `-s a` stamp no trailer, so it changes nothing there

      --dry-run
          Dry run: show what would be done without executing

          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

content.content:
409	### land lands @- by default
410	
411	(wink + agent, 2026-10-29) `land`'s `--source` defaults to "the one local bookmark besides
412	`--onto`", which depends on every bookmark in the repo and fails once there are two. The rest of
413	vc-x1 works from the line's `@-`, `push` moving its bookmark there and `commit --closing` naming it.
414	
415	- `--source` left out is `@-`, with the work `@` empty: what lands is then the tree validation ran
416	  on, and nothing uncommitted is left behind. `commit --closing` without `--land` leaves exactly
417	  this, the closing at `@-` and an empty `@`.
418	- A non-empty work `@` is refused, naming `--source`, rather than warned about, since a land is
419	  pushed and permanent on the trunk. A merge `@`, whose `@-` is ambiguous, is refused too.
420	- The empty check is the work-repo's alone: the agent `@` holds the session and is never empty.
421	- An explicit `--source` lands what it names, with no check of `@`.
422	- The cycle's bookmark is found from `@-` as today: its own, else its nearest parent's above
423	  `--onto`, several refused with the list.
424	- The help: `--source <BM|REV>`, "The cycle's last commit, a bookmark or a revision [default: @-,
425	  with @ empty]".
426

472	### commit --closing reads the nearest opening's title
473	
474	(wink + agent, 2026-10-26) Without `--title`, `commit --closing` takes the cycle title from the
475	opening above the trunk, and with cycles stacked on one line it reads the oldest: the closing of
476	**feat: vc-x1 land** came out as **feat: vc-x1 commit takes a revision closing**, the stack's first
477	cycle, and was made with `--title`.
478	
479	- The opening read is the nearest below the tip, the cycle's own, so a stack closes its top cycle.
480	- A test closes a stack of two cycles without `--title`.
481	
482	### commit --closing merges onto the cycle's base when it was opened above the trunk
483	
484	(wink + agent, 2026-10-26) `commit --closing` merges the trunk with the tip, so a cycle opened
485	above the trunk, on an unlanded series as **feat: vc-x1 land** was, gets a closing whose first
486	parent is the trunk, and the cycles below it leave `main`'s first parents for the second parent's
487	ladder. That closing was re-parented by hand onto the fix commit its opening sat on.
488	
489	- The first parent is the opening's parent, where the cycle's bookmark was created, when that
490	  descends from the trunk, and the trunk otherwise, so `git log --first-parent` reads one commit
491	  per cycle.
492	- A test closes a cycle opened above an unlanded one and checks both parents.
493

149	### install has a role and a profile
150	
151	(wink + agent, 2026-10-30) `[profile.dev]` holds both how a binary is built and what it is installed
152	as, so `vc-x1-dev` reads as the `dev` profile. Wink's model: they are two choices. The profile is how
153	it is compiled, `target/<profile>/<name>`, the name from `Cargo.toml`. The role is what it is: bare
154	`vc-x1` the released version and `vc-x1-dev` the development version, either from any profile.
155	`build` and `run` take a profile alone, and `install` alone has a role. Historically the install was
156	`cargo install --path . --locked`, sometimes with `--root` and a copy, before profiles existed.
157	
158	A proposal, the agent's, wink's to try (2026-10-30):
159	
160	- `[role.released]`, `default-profile = "release"`, and `[role.development]`, `suffix = "-dev"` and
161	  `default-profile = "dev"`. `suffix` leaves `[profile.*]`, and `[install] commands` says
162	  `{role.suffix}`.
163	- `install --as released|development`, the default the running binary's role by its name, so
164	  `vc-x1-dev install` stays development, and `--profile` overrides the role's default.
165	- A released install refuses a dirty build, a commit not on `main`, and a suffixed version unless
166	  `--force`, where today it only reports them. A development install reports them.
167	- The copy stays configured: `[install] commands` holds `cp {profile.bin}` and `mv`, or a project may
168	  list `cargo install --path . --locked --profile {profile.cargo} --root <dir>` and copy from
169	  `<dir>/bin`, which needs no path rule and, by cargo's help, shares the workspace's target directory.
170	  `bin` stays either way, since `run` needs it and `[build] commands` is not cargo-specific.
171	- A config with `suffix` under a profile is refused naming the move, or read as the role's for a
172	  while. Open.
173	
174	### desc takes a title, body, and trailers
175	
176	(wink + agent, 2026-10-30) Overwriting a commit's description takes three commands and leaves gaps:
177	`squash --title --body` on `@-` alone, needing both and folding `@`, `fix-desc --title` with no body
178	and only on a commit whose `ochid:` has an issue, and a hand-run `jj describe` for a trailer or a title. Wink's: `vc-x1 desc` gains optional `--title`, `--body`,
179	`--ochid`, and `--ocid`, in any combination, what is left out kept. With none it reads as it does
180	today. The agent's, to be agreed:
181	
182	- A write requires `-r`, one commit in one repo, so a default of `@` or a range writes nothing by
183	  accident, and `-s both` is refused, each repo's trailers being its own.
184	- `--ochid` repeats and replaces every `ochid:` line, since a Land's agent commit carries several, and
185	  `--ocid ""` removes the line.
186	- Only the description changes, nothing folds, and the tree is checked unchanged.
187	- A published commit is refused unless `--yes`, and `--dry-run` prints the result.
188	- `squash --title --body` and `fix-desc --title` then retire, and `commit -r`'s refusal names `desc`.
189	
190	### init defaults to --local
191	
192	(wink, 2026-10-30) `vc-x1 init` makes the workspace on the machine and creates and publishes nothing
193	unless `--push` asks, as `commit` does in **Only push publishes**. Today it creates the remotes and
194	pushes, public on GitHub unless `--private`, so a bare `init` publishes a repo.
195	
196	- `--push` is what creates the remotes and publishes, and the approval it needs is the rest of that
197	  section's. `--private` and `--push-retries` take effect with it.
198	- Publishing later needs a way: a workspace with no `origin` has nothing for `vc-x1 push` to push to,
199	  so `push`, or a command of its own, creates the remotes.
200	- The trailers: `init`'s cross-links then have no URL to stamp, so they take the path form **feat:
201	  ochid trailers are URLs** defines, `/.agent-session/<chid>`, and they stay valid after a remote
202	  appears, the URL being checked only on a URL form.
203	- The name: `--repo local` is already a category, a local directory of bare repos, which is a remote
204	  of a kind and not this `--local`, so one of the two is renamed or explained. `clone` is to be
205	  checked for the same default.

Land a cycle whose last commit is already made, on the machine: the
agent `@` committed when the cycle's commits name it, the links they
carry updated, --onto fast-forwarded to --source, and the cycle's
bookmark deleted, every check made before anything moves. --push also
publishes it, the agent repo first, and deletes the bookmark on
`origin`. `commit --closing ... --land` lands the same way, the
closing made first.

--source is a bookmark, the cycle's, or a revision, whose current
bookmark, else its nearest parent's above --onto, is the cycle's,
several refused with the list. Left out, it is the one local
bookmark besides --onto. --onto is a local bookmark at its
`origin` position that --source descends from, so a bushy tree lands
anywhere, and Land only fast-forwards: a merge is `commit
--closing`'s. --skip keeps a side of the cycle's bookmark, `local`,
`remote`, or `both`, and --delete-intermediate-bookmarks deletes the
bookmarks strictly between --onto and --source too. --dry-run makes
every check and says each step.

-s is required: `b` a dual workspace, the agent `main` moved with
the trunk, and `p` a plain repo. `w` alone could publish
trailers naming agent commits not yet published, and `a` alone has
no cycle to land, so both are refused. The install stays `vc-x1
install`, after.

Commit the working copies as a rung's pair, one commit per repo of a
dual workspace, each stamped with the other's change id, and with
--push publish it in the same invocation, as `vc-x1 push` would.

The diff and the description are reviewed before the commit, so the
push publishes what was reviewed. It stays on the machine unless
--push asks, for a look at it by `vc-x1 show -s both @-` before
`vc-x1 push`. --local says so outright.

-r REV is the commit the description is for: `@` by default,
committed as the working copy, else `@-` or any draft below it,
described in place with no new commit and its trailer stamped, so a
commit made by hand becomes a rung's. A draft below `@-` is kept
local, since push publishes `@-`. Every argument is a flag: the old
positional is refused, naming -r.

--closing <BM|REV> closes the cycle whose tip it names, onto the trunk,
--land's or `[cycle] trunk`, `main` when absent: one commit above the
trunk is finalized in place, more get the closing commit, the merge of
the trunk and the tip. A tip that is not @- is closed by a detour, @
moving onto it and returning after. --land [TRUNK] lands it: the trunk
fast-forwarded and pushed and the closing's bookmark deleted, every
check first: the one named, or for a revision the current or nearest
parent bookmark above the trunk, several refused with the list.

-s is required: `b` makes both commits now, `w` the work half with
the agent half left to push, `a` the agent repo alone, unpaired, with
no trailer, and `p` a plain repo with no trailer. -R is optional and
says where. --body is the text, or @PATH to read it from a file.

#### Only push publishes

- A bare `vc-x1 commit`, with or without `--land`, and `vc-x1 land`, which is exactly like it, are
  local and need no approval. `vc-x1 push`, exactly like `commit --push`, publishes and needs approval
  unless `--yes`, wink's (2026-10-30). `squash-push` publishes too.
- `[commit] push` goes, so no workspace setting changes what a bare `commit` does.
- `land --push` and `commit --land --push` publish in one step, as `commit --push` does, and delete
  the published bookmark on `origin`, built in **feat: improve trailers**.
- Open: the approval's mechanism. We think it is the Bash hook sending what publishes to the
  permission prompt, since an agent can type `--yes` as easily as anything else. And a bare Land's
  deletion of a published bookmark, which is itself publishing, so `land` deletes the local one and
  `delete-bookmark` the remote one today, wink's preference being that `push` does.

##### Why: only push publishes

A local commit can be reworked and a push cannot easily be taken back, so the safe act is the one
done by doing nothing, and publishing has one place to gate.

#### A cycle stays local until its Land

On trial, from **feat: improve trailers**, wink's (2026-10-30), and the cycle of record if
that cycle's Land works. A new cycle type, for every cycle and not that one alone.

- Every commit is the work half alone, made and kept local: `commit -s w`, the opening's bookmark
  created and not pushed. The agent `@` is neither committed nor pushed before the Land, so
  its change id holds for the whole cycle.
- The work review stays on every commit. The description review goes, wink's (2026-10-30), since a
  local description can still be changed before the Land. Approval per push reduces to one go, the
  Land's.
- The Land commits the agent `@` first, one `ochid:` per work commit, sets each work commit's `ocid:`
  to its SHA and each `pcid:` to its parent's new SHA, trees unchanged, all on the machine. `push -s b --bookmark <TRUNK>` then pushes
  the agent repo first and the work repo after. It folds nothing into the agent commit, so the SHA
  every `ocid:` names holds, and what arrives after it rides the next cycle's agent commit.
- Each rung's `ochid:` is the same agent change, so it stays right when the Land commits it, and only
  `ocid:` and `pcid:` are written then.
- No `squash-push -s a`: At rest's item 2 goes, and "clean" means the work `@` is empty, the agent's
  `@` being the session's data and no finding, as [Acquaint](AGENTS.md#acquaint) says.
- A single-step cycle is the same with one commit.
- A rung that changes the code ends with `vc-x1 install --profile dev`, after validate, wink's
  (2026-10-30), so the next rung runs the code just reviewed.
- The sections it rewrites: Opening step 2, the per-rung flow's step 9, Committing vs pushing, At
  rest, Before any push, and Land. It replaces **A local commit pair before every push** above, a
  rung no longer making a pair, and Every cycle starts with `commit --opening` holds with the
  bookmark local.
- Open:
  - One machine: a local cycle cannot move between machines or survive a lost disk. We think an
    explicit backup push of the work bookmark answers it, and that runs into the rule that what is
    published names nothing unpublished, and into the Land rewriting those commits.
  - Shared repos: **Cycles in a shared repo, by fork and pull request** needs a branch pushed before

content.text:
The reordered file drops most of `TODO.md`, so it can't replace it as it stands. The work-repo ladder is linear. I've changed nothing since the `zDOING.md` edit, and my recommendation is at the end.

## `../TODO.md.vc-x1`
It looks like a copy cut off partway through the v0.3.1 entry, then reordered.

| | Count | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| `TODO.md` entries | 116 | |
| Reordered file entries | 23 | 22 shared, plus your renamed one |
| Dropped entries | 93 | everything after v0.3.1, including **Parallel cycles** and **feat: vc-x1 msg** |
| Dropped sections | 3 | `## Waiting`, `## Ideas`, `# References` |
| **v0.3.1 lines** | 358 → 7 | everything from `#### Never rename` on is gone, which is the proposal itself |

Other differences in the 22 shared entries:
- **Older text:** it comes from before the rename. It says `feat: ochid trailers are URLs` in two entries and has an older version of **desc takes a title, body, and trailers**.
- **Your additions:** three new `(wink ...)` notes, which I'd keep. One blank line was also added to **squash-push shows what it takes, and push follows jj**.
- **The dogfood rename:** it also removes the rule for making the closing and Land with their own build. The heading's "it's" should be "its".

## Linearity
- **Work-repo:** yes, the ladder is linear. All 11 rungs have one parent, in order, starting from `8be6ff7c`, and author times increase.
- **The 12th commit:** the closing is the trapezoid merge of `8be6ff7c` and the ladder's tip, so `main` itself isn't linear, by design.
- **Agent-repo:** one commit, `a14fd790`, whose 12 `ochid:` lines match the 12 work commits in order. All 12 work commits link back to it.
- **The rewrite at Land:** Land stamped all 12 commits, so their SHAs changed. The commit you tested, `cc4bdf76`, and the landed `4a827490` have the identical tree.

The cost of this model is that one agent commit covers the whole cycle, so `lookup` is less precise per rung. It also makes the agent commit large, which the proposal already lists as open.

## The closing anomaly
I take this to be the following; correct me if you meant something else. The agent commit only exists at Land, so a closed cycle still carries `ocid: .../xxxx`, and you can't test a truly final closing. That's also how we ended up with the five-step sequence you rejected.

I'd make each operation do one thing:

| Operation | What it does | Rewrites SHAs? |
|---|---|---|
| **close** | makes the closing and the agent commit, and stamps all the trailers | yes, for the last time |
| *test* | any validate or install | no |
| **land** | fast-forwards the trunk, deletes the local bookmark | no |
| **push** | publishes agent then work, deletes the remote bookmark | no |

- **What you get:** the commit you test is the commit that lands and gets pushed, with the same SHA.
- **The cost:** a transcript written after close goes into the next cycle's agent commit, and reworking after close has to re-stamp the trailers.
- **Making it obvious:** each command ends by printing the cycle's state and the valid next steps, and refuses anything out of order. A one-shot `--land --push` stays available.
- **Fold into this cycle:** **commit --closing reads the nearest opening's title** and **land lands @- by default**.
- **Your question on merging onto the cycle's base:** it only matters when a cycle is opened on top of an unlanded one. Each cycle then keeps its own first-parent line. We think the danger is carrying an unclosed lower cycle onto `main`, so it should refuse unless that cycle is closed. With that guard I'd include it too, which also answers your "should these be one cycle?".

## Testing and the test repo
- **Conflict with a Todo:** you described installing by `profile.<name>.suffix`, but **install has a role and a profile** moves `suffix` out of profiles. If your description stands, that entry should be retired.
- **Validate by profile:** `[validate]` only has `full` and `fast` today, so this would be new.
- **`init --local-test-repo <path>`:** most of it already exists as `init --target <path> --repo local=<parent>`, so it's mainly a shorter spelling, which I'd add.
- **`[repos].test`:** I'd use `[test] repo` beside `fixtures`, a relative path under the gitignored `.fixtures`. `[repos]` lists the workspace's own two repos.
- **No automatic default:** I'd reach the test repo explicitly with `-R`. If `vc-x1-dev` defaulted to it, rungs would stop running on the real repos, which defeats dogfooding.

## Recommended order
1. **Fix the Todo:** a small chore that puts your 23 entries on top in your order and adds your notes and rename. It keeps the current text, v0.3.1's body, and everything else below them.
2. **Close, land, push:** this cycle, with the test repo as its first rung so its acceptance check can run the whole sequence without touching the real repos.
3. **Release v0.3.1:** move it up from 13th to directly after that. Otherwise the 12 entries above it stand between you and io_uring, and the rules would describe a closing that's about to change. The rest of your order stays.

The proposal still has open items to settle at release, including how push approval works. Doing all of this today depends on how large step 2 turns out to be.

## Decisions for you
1. Do you want the 93 dropped entries kept below your 23? I recommend yes. If you meant to trim them, moving them to `notes/todo-backlog.md` keeps them.
2. Is the anomaly the one I described?
3. Does the agent commit move to close, as in the table?
4. Do you want a `vc-x1 close` subcommand? I recommend yes, since it pairs with `land` and `push`, with `commit --closing` sharing its code.
5. Is the role proposal retired in favor of `profile.<name>.suffix`?

The plain version: your new list lost most of the Todo, including the content of v0.3.1, so I'd apply your order to the real file instead. The ladder is linear. Next I'd make close do all the final stamping, so that what you test is exactly what lands, then release v0.3.1.

vc-x1 0.85.18+4a827490b131

Rewrite a range of work commits' trailers to what is stamped today,
only their descriptions changing, each tree checked unchanged.

`ochid:` becomes the partner's bare change id. `ocid:` links the agent
commit by its SHA, or the placeholder `xxxx` while it is the
uncommitted agent `@`. `pcid:` links each parent by its SHA, one line
per parent in parent order, so the range goes oldest first. Links use
the `origin`'s canonical URL, or `file:///` for a local one. A trailer
naming nothing that resolves, a `lost` or an old short id, is left as
it is, and a trailer `vc-x1` does not stamp is kept.

--update is required, the one thing this does so far. --range is a
bookmark or revision, those above the trunk up to it, or a revset with
`..` or `::`, as written [default: above the trunk up to `@-`]. A
commit on the trunk's remote is refused without --yes, and one on a
topic bookmark is rewritten with a warning. --dry-run prints each
description, parents at their current SHAs. The work repo alone
changes, an agent commit carrying only change ids.

Usage: vc-x1 trailers [OPTIONS] --update

Options:
      --update
          Rewrite the trailers, the one thing this does so far

  -V, --version...
          Version detail on stdout: -V the banner, -VV the full report (as
          `vc-x1 version`). Counted like -v/-vv.
          
          Both ride along: they print, then the subcommand runs, so one
          invocation captures the version and the command's output together.
          That is why this replaces clap's auto-version, which would exit after
          printing. Without either, the banner still prints, on stderr.

      --no-banner
          Suppress the banner stderr normally carries on every run.
          
          Only the ambient banner: an explicit `-V` still prints, since asking
          for it outranks suppressing it.

      --range <BM|REV>
          The commits: a bookmark or revision, those above the trunk up to it,
          or a revset with `..` or `::`, as written [default: those above the
          trunk up to `@-`]

      --allow-jj-mismatch
          Run even when `jj -V` disagrees with our linked jj-lib.
          
          Per-invocation on purpose, never a config key: a key gets set once
          during a frustrating afternoon and then silently protects nothing.

      --yes
          Rewrite a commit already on the trunk's remote, which is refused
          without it

  -R, --repo <PATH>
          Where: a path in the workspace, its root or either repo [default: the
          current directory]

  -v, --verbose...
          Verbose output: -v debug, -vv trace

      --dry-run
          Dry run: show what would be done without executing

      --log <LOG>
          Log file path (captures all levels)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

487	### lookup
488	
489	Show the lines in the other repo that a line in this one relates to. `vc-x1 lookup [-s SCOPE]
490	--line FILE:LINE` takes a line as an editor, a compiler, or grep prints it, places the file on one
491	side of the workspace, and resolves it to the window on the other side, work-to-transcript or
492	transcript-to-work. The requirements are in [What the lookup command
493	needs](notes/transcript-write.md#what-the-lookup-command-needs).
494	
495	- `-s`/`--scope` is the side the line is on, `work` or `agent`. Omitted, it is inferred from the
496	  file's path. Named, a `FILE` that does not exist relative to the current directory is taken
497	  relative to that side's repo root, so a repo-relative path works from anywhere once the side is
498	  said. A named side the path disagrees with is an error, never a hint.
499	- `--line FILE:LINE` splits at its last colon, so a path holding a colon still parses, and the line
500	  must exist in the file on disk. The old `[SCOPE] FILE:LINE` positionals are refused, naming `-s`
501	  and `--line`.
502	- The workspace is `-R`/`--repo` when given, else found from the file.
503	- `-r`/`--revision REV` reads the line from the file as of REV instead of from disk, for a line
504	  the working copy no longer holds, such as a cycle-record line the next opening deleted.
505	
506	A work line prints the commit it arrived in, blamed at the working copy after a snapshot, and
507	that commit's partner by its `ochid:` trailer. When the line moved, the commit that first wrote
508	it and that commit's partner follow. A commit with no trailer prints its candidate partners, the
509	agent commits within `--tolerance` seconds of it, 60 by default, nearest first:
510	
511	```
512	work TODO.md:21
513	    The first decision needs revising.

515	written yuoqvtxvozko fix: the design note opening
516	partner vxkqvspultnv fix: the design note closing
517	written partner qxqzomnwkonk fix: the design note opening
518	```
519	
520	An agent line, a session file's line, prints as the rendered transcript entry, then the agent
521	commit that appended it, blamed at the agent repo's working copy after a snapshot, and every work
522	commit that commit's `ochid:` trailers name, the work commits its push published. Each work
523	commit's diff is the window, printed as `FILE:START-END` regions with their removed and added
524	lines. When the line is a transcript write the window narrows to the files it wrote, one for a
525	`Write` or `Edit` and every changed file a `Bash` command names, and any other line is discussion

### lookup

Show the lines in the other repo that a line in this one relates to. `vc-x1 lookup [-s SCOPE]
--line FILE:LINE` takes a line as an editor, a compiler, or grep prints it, places the file on one
side of the workspace, and resolves it to the window on the other side, work-to-transcript or
transcript-to-work. The requirements are in [What the lookup command
needs](notes/transcript-write.md#what-the-lookup-command-needs).

- `-s`/`--scope` is the side the line is on, `work` or `agent`. Omitted, it is inferred from the
  file's path. Named, a `FILE` that does not exist relative to the current directory is taken
  relative to that side's repo root, so a repo-relative path works from anywhere once the side is
  said. A named side the path disagrees with is an error, never a hint.
- `--line FILE:LINE` splits at its last colon, so a path holding a colon still parses, and the line
  must exist in the file on disk. The old `[SCOPE] FILE:LINE` positionals are refused, naming `-s`
  and `--line`.
- The workspace is `-R`/`--repo` when given, else found from the file.
- `-r`/`--revision REV` reads the line from the file as of REV instead of from disk, for a line
  the working copy no longer holds, such as a cycle-record line the next opening deleted.

A work line prints the commit it arrived in, blamed at the working copy after a snapshot, and
that commit's partner by its `ochid:` trailer. When the line moved, the commit that first wrote
it and that commit's partner follow. A commit with no trailer prints its candidate partners, the
agent commits within `--tolerance` seconds of it, 60 by default, nearest first:

```
work TODO.md:21
    The first decision needs revising.
commit  kxpuoxoznwyn TODO.md:21 fix: the design note closing
written yuoqvtxvozko fix: the design note opening
partner vxkqvspultnv fix: the design note closing
written partner qxqzomnwkonk fix: the design note opening
```

commit that appended it, blamed at the agent repo's working copy after a snapshot, and every work
commit that commit's `ochid:` trailers name, the work commits its push published. Each work
commit's diff is the window, printed as `FILE:START-END` regions with their removed and added
lines. When the line is a transcript write the window narrows to the files it wrote, one for a
`Write` or `Edit` and every changed file a `Bash` command names, and any other line is discussion
and takes the diff whole. A line not yet pushed says so:

lastPrompt: I copied the above to ./tmp/agent-response-2026-11-02.txt so I can read it in a separate window and we can discuss various sections. Glad it's linear, but how onerous is the single agent-repo commit.…

content.text:
**I wouldn't discourage the single agent commit.** Only two costs are real, and one of them is cheap to fix. Non-linear work is mostly not a problem, because the two repos are linked by id, not by position, until someone rewrites history outside jj.

## How onerous is it?
I measured last cycle's commit, `a14fd790`, and ran `lookup` on it:

| Concern | Result | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | 11.6 MB, 4,238 lines, one file; the repo is already 931 MB | Little: the transcript exists either way, so we think the total barely changes |
| Work line → transcript | `src/desc_helpers.rs:232` found its exact `Edit` at line 1260 | None |
| Transcript line → work | line 1200 returned all 12 work commits and 6,372 lines of output | **Real** |
| Durability | three days of rungs and transcript existed only on this machine | **Real**, and already an open item in the proposal |
| jj's 1 MiB new-file limit | yours is off (`max-new-file-size = "0"`), but the default refuses a new file over the limit | A possible trap for adopters if the transcript is first snapshotted late |

The benefit is also real. Last cycle inserted rungs, removed a closing and renamed itself, and none of that disturbed a published link, because nothing was published.

**The transcript → work loss looks fixable:** when `commit -s w` makes a rung, it could record the transcript's current line number. The rung's span would then be known without a separate agent commit. It should be a line number, not a time, because 93 transcript entries are out of time order. Rework done later would blur the spans a little. I haven't built or tried this.

**Durability needs its own answer:** a backup push of the work bookmark would publish trailers naming an agent commit that doesn't exist yet, and Land would rewrite those commits anyway. The simplest answer may be a backup of the two repos to a local or private remote, which isn't the project's `origin`.

**When to use which:**
- **Single agent commit (default):** one person on one machine, where the design may still move.
- **A pair per rung:** the cycle needs to be visible while it runs, or it moves between machines.

## How hard is non-linear work?
The agent-repo's order is just time, and the work-repo's is a graph. They don't have to match. What matters is which trailer each operation breaks:

| Operation | `ochid` work → agent | `ochid` agent → work | `ocid` agent SHA | `pcid` parent SHA |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| jj rebase or reorder | fine | fine | fine | stale, `trailers --update` fixes it |
| jj merge | fine | fine | fine | one per parent, stamped at commit or by `trailers --update` |
| jj squash, before Land | fine | fine, Land writes the list from the current commits | fine | stale, then fixed |
| jj squash, after the agent commit exists | fine | **dangling for the lost id** | fine | stale, then fixed |
| Git or GitHub rebase merge | fine if the message is kept | **dangling** | fine | stale |
| GitHub squash merge | only if the trailers survive in the message | **dangling** | only if the trailers survive | gone |

So the difficulty falls into three levels:
- **Easy:** any reshaping in jj before Land, which is where the local model helps. Land links whatever commits exist at that moment, so there's nothing to coordinate.
- **Moderate:** reshaping after the agent commit exists. It needs a re-stamp, and if close makes the agent commit, as I proposed earlier, then rework after close lands here. So `close` must be safe to re-run.
- **Hard:** rewrites outside jj, or a squash merge in a shared repo. The ids are gone, and no bookkeeping can restore them.

The hard case already has a planned answer in `## Waiting`: **lookup matches a line to its write by content**. The `Edit` lookup found above shows the transcript holds what it needs, but today that search runs only inside the window the trailer gives. It would have to work across every session, which is the indexing and privacy problem that entry describes.

**One caveat:** the table comes from reading the code and docs. I didn't run these operations, and **lookup is tested on a reordered ladder** is still an open Todo. If you want this settled, the test repo from the close cycle is the place to run each row as a table-driven test.

## What I'd do
1. Keep local-until-Land as the default in v0.3.1, and keep a pair per rung as a documented alternative.
2. Add the line-number mark, and make `close` safe to re-run, both in the close cycle.
3. Leave the backup question and the GitHub merge cases out of v0.3.1. They belong to **Cycles in a shared repo, by fork and pull request**, so they shouldn't delay io_uring.

The plain version: one big agent commit costs almost nothing in storage or in tracing code back to the conversation. It makes tracing a conversation forward to code imprecise, and everything sits on one machine until Land. Reordering or merging in jj is easy, since a re-stamp fixes it. Only rewrites outside jj, such as a GitHub squash merge, truly break the links, and that's a shared-repo problem for later.

message.content: I also, want to note my thinking is we'll have a TUI/GUI with at least two windows, one for the work and agent, and those should be linear/correlated? I would also expect that the UI app would build an "index" to efficiently correlate the two sides.

content.text:
That fits, and it changes one of my recommendations: **I'd drop the line-number mark**, because a UI index can derive the same information. I'd also keep the two panes correlated without requiring them to share one order.

## Linear and correlated
Each pane can be linear on its own terms, but the two orders can legitimately differ:
- **Agent pane:** the transcript in file order, which is always a single line.
- **Work pane:** the commits flattened into one line, with merges drawn as markers.
- **Correlation:** transcript spans mapped to work commits, not agent commits to work commits. With one agent commit per cycle, only spans give a useful link.

After a reorder, or when rework lands in an earlier rung, the links between panes would cross. I'd show that crossing, because it's true and useful: the conversation happened in one order and the commits ended up in another. A merge shows up the same way.

## The index
I'd make it a derived, disposable cache: gitignored, rebuildable from the repos at any time, and never the source of truth. Transcripts only grow, so updates can be incremental.

It would combine evidence in order of strength:
1. **Trailers**, when they resolve.
2. **Commit calls in the transcript**, for rung boundaries.
3. **Content**, matching what each `Write` and `Edit` put into a file against the lines in each commit.
4. **Time**, as a last resort.

Layer 3 is the same work as **lookup matches a line to its write by content** in `## Waiting`, so the UI index would also address the hard case from my last message. A GitHub squash merge loses the ids, but the text still matches. The fuzzy matching and the privacy question in that entry stay open.

## Why the mark can go
I checked whether rung boundaries are already recoverable from last cycle's transcript, and **all 12 rungs' commit calls are there**, from line 1188 to line 4572.

Recovering them isn't just a search, though:
- **False hits:** dry runs, retries, and a first closing at line 3897 that was later removed.
- **Retitled commits:** the opening still carries its old title, **feat: ochid trailers are URLs**.
- **Buried calls:** one commit is inside a compound command at line 4145.
- **Commits outside the session:** a commit you run in your own terminal isn't in the transcript, so that case falls back to content and time. The final `land --push` was like that.

I only confirmed the calls can be found; I haven't built an index or measured its accuracy. A stamp would add a field to every commit to save work the index has to be able to do anyway.

## What this means for today
Nothing here blocks v0.3.1 or the close cycle, and neither needs to build any of it. Three points do follow:
- **Close cycle:** it gets smaller, since making `close` safe to re-run stays but the mark goes.
- **Local-until-Land:** this strengthens the case for keeping it. The main cost of one agent commit was imprecise transcript → work lookup, and the index removes that.
- **Keep the evidence intact:** the design depends on complete transcripts and on trailers that stay accurate, so no rule should trim or rewrite transcripts. I don't see anything in v0.3.1 that does, but I've only read parts of that proposal closely, so I'll check when we get to it.

The viewer already appears in `TODO.md`: the `## Waiting` entry on retiring frozen history, **lookup --history**, and **Chores retire into a session index (post-viewer)**. When we run the Todo fix, I'll add this design to one new entry that links to those, rather than scattering it.

The plain version: the UI shows two timelines with lines linking conversation spans to commits, and those lines may cross. A throwaway index works out the links from trailers, commit calls, matching text and time. So we don't need to stamp anything extra now, and today's plan gets slightly smaller.

(wink + agent, 2026-11-02) The hypothesis, wink's: with an index, one agent commit per cycle and one
per rung make no difference to correlating the two repos, so `lookup` builds the index in
`<path>/agent-repo-indexes/`, and it is tested with no UI. A lookup from a transcript line today
returns every work commit its agent commit names, 12 commits and 6,372 lines of output for line 1200
of `520a2a50-1afc-4282-a824-bc78c27b7cc5.jsonl`.

- What it maps: transcript spans to work commits, not agent commits to work commits.
- The evidence, strongest first:
  - the trailers, when they resolve
  - the commit calls in the transcript, for rung boundaries
  - the content each `Write` and `Edit` put into a file, matched against each commit's lines
  - time, last, since a Land rewrites committer time and we think only author time holds
- What it is: a cache, rebuildable from the repos at any time and never the source of truth.
  Transcripts only grow, so we think it updates incrementally.
- Where it lives: `<path>` is open. Anything inside the agent-repo's tree gets committed with the
  session, so it is outside that tree or gitignored there.
- The rung boundaries are not a plain search. All 12 of **feat: improve trailers**'s commit calls are
  in its transcript, among dry runs, retries, a removed first closing at line 3897, an opening under
  its old title, and one inside a compound command at line 4145. A commit run outside the session,
  as that cycle's `land --push` was, is not in the transcript at all.
- The test, on real cycles:
  - A cycle committed per rung is the ground truth: build its index with its trailers ignored and
    compare each span's work commit with what the trailer says, **feat: build, install, and run take
    --profile** one candidate.
  - **feat: improve trailers**, one agent commit for 12 work commits, then gets the same queries, and
    each answer is checked against its rung's diff.
  - A count of wrong, ambiguous, and missing answers is the result, and it says whether the
    hypothesis holds.
- Outside the hypothesis: an index does not change what one agent commit means for durability, since
  a cycle's transcript and rungs still sit on one machine until the Land.
- What it unblocks: the TUI or GUI, wink's thinking (2026-11-02), at least two windows, the work and
  the agent, each linear and correlated by this index, with links that cross where the conversation's
  order and the commits' order differ. Related:
  - **lookup matches a line to its write by content** in `## Waiting`, whose matching is the third
    layer here, its fuzzy matching and privacy questions still open
  - **lookup --history steps a region through the commits that changed it**
  - **Chores retire into a session index (post-viewer)**

import re
import sys

todo_path, mine_path = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
OLD_DOGFOOD = "### agent-files(proposal): a cycle is made by its own build"
MINE_DOGFOOD = "### A cycle should dogfood it's own changes continuously"
NEW_DOGFOOD = "### A cycle should dogfood its own changes continuously"
V031 = "### agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1"
INDEX = "### lookup builds an index that correlates the two repos"
TAIL = "### squash and commit take --exclude"
NOTED = {
    "### commit works at every scope, and --local keeps it on the machine",
    "### commit --closing reads the nearest opening's title",
    "### commit --closing merges onto the cycle's base when it was opened above the trunk",
}


def blocks(lines):
    """Split into a head and (heading, lines) entries at each ### outside a fence."""
    head, out, fence = [], [], False
    for line in lines:
        if line.startswith("```"):
            fence = not fence
        if not fence and line.startswith("### "):
            out.append((line, [line]))
        elif out:
            out[-1][1].append(line)
        else:
            head.append(line)
    return head, out

lines = text.split("\n")
tail_at = lines.index(TAIL)
head, old = blocks(lines[:tail_at])
old_map = dict(old)
_, mine = blocks(open(mine_path, encoding="utf-8").read().rstrip("\n").split("\n"))
mine_map = dict(mine)

result = list(head)
for heading, _ in mine:
    if heading == MINE_DOGFOOD:
        body = [l.rstrip() for l in mine_map[heading][1:]]
        while body and body[-1] == "":
            body.pop()
        result += [NEW_DOGFOOD] + body + [""]
        continue
    block = list(old_map[heading])
    if heading in NOTED:
        # The note is what the reordered copy has between the heading and the entry's text.
        first = old_map[heading][2]
        note = mine_map[heading][1 : mine_map[heading].index(first) - 1]
        block = [heading] + note + block[1:]
    result += block
    if heading == V031:
        result += old_map[INDEX]

expected = {h for h, _ in old} - {OLD_DOGFOOD}
placed = {h for h, _ in mine} - {MINE_DOGFOOD} | {INDEX}
if expected != placed:
    sys.exit(f"entries differ: {sorted(expected ^ placed)}")

result += lines[tail_at:]
open(todo_path, "w", encoding="utf-8").write("\n".join(result))
print(f"{len(lines)} lines before, {len(result)} after")

LG, txs for merging that. Let's start a new cycle I think with one more todo, fixing "The closing anomaly".
One thing in your table, my read is that "close" implies commiting agent so there is a cid (sha). That isn't what I want because after closing I want to be able to have the agent do more tweaking. So in a protocol where there are multi work-repo commits and one agent-repo commit closing has to have two phases. Create it's final form (single-step or multi-step trapezoidal) with the ochid and pcid but the ocid is its reference slug is "xxxx". This allows the agent and user to iterate the work-repo changes. These work-repo commits will be --local by default but can be pushed if desired for durability without any consequences, I think. Thougths only.

You're right, and I withdraw the agent commit at close. Your version is better for three reasons:
- **Same agent commit:** the conversation from your tweaking goes into the cycle's own agent commit, not the next cycle's.
- **Free rework:** nothing names the rungs from the agent side yet, so rework after close is as cheap as rework before it.
- **Less to re-stamp:** the moderate case I listed earlier, reshaping after the agent commit exists, mostly disappears.

## The two phases
They fit the three operations you already listed, with no new command:

| Operation | What it does | Can you still iterate? |
|---|---|---|
| **close** | makes the final shape, with `ochid`, `pcid`, and `ocid: .../xxxx` | Yes, freely, and it can be pushed |
| **land** | commits the agent `@`, sets every `ocid`, refreshes every `pcid`, fast-forwards the trunk locally | Only by undoing it |
| **push** | publishes agent then work, deletes the remote bookmark | No |

Land is the second phase, so testing has two levels:
- **After close:** the tree is what you're testing. Land only changes descriptions, and last cycle's closing kept an identical tree through it.
- **After land, before push:** the exact final SHAs. This matters a little because the binary's version embeds the SHA, as `vc-x1` at `+4a827490` and `vc-x1-dev` at `+cc4bdf76` show. It's also the last-test point you asked for last session.

This is close to what the code did last cycle, so the fix may be smaller than I implied. I haven't checked how much already holds; that's the first job of the cycle.

## Pushing with `xxxx`
Solo, I agree it's harmless to a closed cycle, with these caveats:
- **Land rewrites what you pushed:** every SHA changes, so the next push of that bookmark is a force-push. `trailers` already warns when it rewrites a commit on a topic bookmark.
- **Old links die:** any `pcid` URL or SHA you copied from a pushed version stops pointing at the live branch.
- **Renames leave litter:** renaming the cycle leaves the old bookmark on `origin`, as `feat-ochid-trailers-are-urls` did last cycle.
- **Shared repos:** force-pushes affect anyone who fetched the branch, so this is only clean for now.
- **Durability is half solved:** the work commits are backed up, but the transcript still sits on one machine until Land.

## What needs guarding
- **`xxxx` reaching the trunk:** that would be permanent. `push` should refuse a trunk commit that still has the placeholder, in case Land was skipped or `main` was moved by hand. This is the most important guard, and I don't yet know whether one exists.
- **The agent `@` being committed mid-cycle:** `squash-push -s a` or `commit -s b` would split the transcript and leave Land unsure what to commit. These should refuse or warn while a closed cycle names that `@`.
- **The trunk moving during iteration:** Land only fast-forwards, so the closing's merge has to be redone. That's why close still has to be safe to re-run.
- **Stale `pcid` during iteration:** a tweak below the closing makes every `pcid` above it wrong until Land refreshes them. `validate-desc` shouldn't report that as a failure at this stage, or the check will become noise.
- **Saying where you are:** each command should end by printing the state and the valid next steps, which is your "obvious" requirement.

## The cycle I'd open
**Title:** something like `fix: close, land, and push say where a cycle is`.

It would start by running the sequence on a test repo to see what already works, then fix what doesn't. It would fold in the two `commit --closing` entries and **land lands @- by default**, and include the test repo and the guards above. A `vc-x1 close` subcommand would be part of it if you still want one.

**Your decision:** does land stay the seal, as in the table? I recommend yes. A separate seal command would only add a step you've already said you don't want.

The plain version: close stays fully editable with `xxxx` as a placeholder, and land fills in the real ids and moves the trunk locally, leaving one last test before push. Pushing a closed cycle for backup is fine when you're solo, as long as `xxxx` can never reach `main`.

content.text:
I agree: the id should become permanent when work reaches the release line, not at land. That's the moment that's actually permanent; every land before it stays local and reworkable.

## The revised model

| Operation | Repos | What it does | `ocid` |
|---|---|---|---|
| **close** | work | makes the final shape | `xxxx` |
| **land** | work | merges or fast-forwards onto any bookmark; can repeat | `xxxx` |
| **push** to a topic bookmark | work | shares it for backup or for others to test | `xxxx` |
| **push** to the release line | both | seals: commits the agent `@`, sets `ocid`, refreshes `pcid`, publishes agent then work | real SHA |

What gets better:
- **Land is simpler:** it no longer touches the agent-repo, so `land -s w` becomes the normal form, not a refused one.
- **`xxxx` guards itself:** vc-x1's own push can't publish it to the release line, because that push is the step that replaces it. A raw `jj git push` could still do it.
- **One approval:** there's one go, and a dry run can show every rewrite before it happens.

## What it costs
- **No final-SHA test before release:** the last-test point I described between land and push goes away. You'd be relying on the sealed tree being identical, which the seal should check and refuse if not. Only the embedded version string differs, so I think that's acceptable.
- **Testers' SHAs won't match:** someone testing a shared build reports a SHA that never reaches `main`. The change id still ties it to the released commit, but only if we report it.
- **Push now rewrites history:** this bends **Only push publishes**, since one specific push rewrites before it publishes. It should say so plainly, and it should check the push can fast-forward before committing anything.
- **The install moves:** a released binary with the final SHA can only be built after that push, so the install has to come after it.

## Cases this creates
- **PR merges:** in a fork-and-PR flow, GitHub does the merge to `main`, so no vc-x1 push ever happens there. Sealing has to be callable on its own, before the PR. So I'd build it as a separate internal step that this push runs, with its own flag.
- **Several cycles in one seal:** a stack landed together shares one agent `@`, so one agent commit covers them all. Its title can't just come from "the closing", so it needs a rule.
- **Someone else's commits:** a range can include `xxxx` commits naming a different agent `@`, after a merge or rebase. The seal should refuse those, since it can't supply their SHA.
- **A longer exposed window:** the agent `@` can now stay uncommitted across several lands, which makes the guard against committing it mid-cycle more important.

## Rewrite one commit, not twelve
The `ocid` is the only reason every rung gets rewritten at the seal, and the `pcid` refresh only follows from that. If only the **closing** carried `ocid`:
- The seal would rewrite just that one commit.
- The rungs would keep their SHAs, so testers' SHAs would match for everything except the closing, and their links would survive.
- `ochid` already identifies the agent commit on every rung, so `lookup` wouldn't need `ocid` there.

The cost is that a GitHub reader on a rung has no clickable link to the agent commit and has to go through the closing. I'd take that trade, though it partly reverses your **Work commits link by URL** decision from last cycle, so it's your call. I'd settle it before building, since it decides how much the seal does.

## Effect on the plan
- **The cycle:** seal-at-push replaces land-as-seal.
- **v0.3.1:** at least **A cycle stays local until its Land**, **Land is the sequence, and `vc-x1 land` its integrate step**, **Only push publishes** and **Work commits link by URL** need rewriting. "Land" also stops being what makes a cycle permanent, so the rules' Terminology needs a word for that step. I'd use "release".

**Your decisions:**
1. Does `ocid` go on every rung or only the closing? I recommend only the closing.
2. What marks the release line: `[cycle] trunk` or a new key? I recommend `[cycle] trunk` until a project actually needs separate release branches.

The plain version: land and sharing stay work-only with `xxxx`, and the one push to `main` fills in the real ids and publishes both repos. You give up testing the exact final SHA, though not the exact final code. If only the closing carries `ocid`, that push rewrites one commit instead of twelve.

But more generally ocid is added to the next work-repo commit following a agent-repo commit. So in
a single agent-repo scenario that's closing, but in our "old" style it's every commit. And it also
