tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

lastPrompt: I think in this cycle we change --use-template. But if we --use-agent-template maybe --use-template changes to --use-work-template then --scope both means use it's .vc-config.md [repos].agent. Another…

content.text:
It isn't too complex, because most of it reuses what `init` already has. I'd make one flag simpler and add one rule, and I agree with doing it in this cycle.

**What fits well**
- **Scope:** `init` already has `-s both|por`, so `both` follows the config to the agent template, and `por` needs no agent template.
- **Lookup:** `--use-work-template <path>` reads the source's `[repos] agent`, which replaces both the `.claude` guess and my `work/` + `agent/` root detection.
- **URLs:** `[remote] agent-repo` exists because `clone` needs it when there's no agent-repo to ask yet, so a URL source can follow the same approach.

**The flag I'd change:** drop `--use-agent-repo`. `--use-agent-template <PATH|URL>` can be the one override for both cases. `init` also already has `--agent-repo`, which names the new workspace's remote, so the two would be easy to confuse.

**The rule it needs:** following `[repos].agent` on a working repo points straight at `.agent-session`, which holds private transcripts. `--use-work-template ~/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1` would also copy `src/` and `TODO.md`.

My earlier test of "has a `.vc-config.md` means working repo" no longer works either, because a template now needs that file too. `vc-x1-template-2/work` doesn't have one yet.

So I'd have the source declare what it gives:
- **With a `[template]` list:** copy the listed files from each repo. A real template declares this.
- **Without one:** copy only the agent-files from the work side and nothing from the agent side, and `vc-x1` supplies the blank `TODO.md` and the other starter files. Your `vc-x1` repo falls in this case.

That makes a working repo safe by default, and a repo only shares more by listing it.

**What I'd do**

| When | What |
|---|---|
| New rung, this cycle | The two flags, replacing `--use-template` and the comma form, plus the config lookup, the `[template]` rule, and a `.vc-config.md` for `vc-x1-template-2` |
| After v0.3.1 | URL sources |

I'd wait on URLs because they add cloning to a temp directory and access to private repos, and you don't need them for io_uring testing. `--use-work-template ~/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1` would work this cycle, but it gets v0.3.0 rules until v0.3.1 is released, so keep using the template for the draft rules.

The plain version: use two flags that each take one path, and let the work template's config say where the agent template is. A repo only gives what it lists, and without a list it gives just its rules, so your transcripts and source can't get copied. Local paths go in this cycle and URLs come after v0.3.1.

message.content: I don't think we should copy TODO.md nor the src/ unless we add flags for that purpose, `init` is not an attpempt to duplicate repos it's for initializing either an empty one or you've done a `cargo init ...` and now you want to turn that into a dual repo. Or the opposite you create a dual repo with `vc-x1 init` and then run `carog init ...` on it. So ATM I see us creating a dual repo that could be use with any programing language.

content.text:
That makes it simpler, and it replaces my `[template]` list and most of the flag design from my last message. If `init` only copies the rules, nothing else needs selecting.

**What `init` makes**
- **Copied from the source:** `AGENTS.md` and `agent-data/`, the same set `vc-x1 agent-files copy` already defines, which leaves out `TODO.md`.
- **Written by `init`:** `.vc-config.md`, `.gitignore`, and new language-neutral starter files: a blank `TODO.md` (the rules require one) and `CLAUDE.md`.
- **Left to the project:** source, `Cargo.toml`, licenses and `[validate]` commands.

**The flags:** with this rule the agent side has nothing to contribute, because its config and `.gitignore` are generated and its transcripts must never be copied. That means one flag is enough:
- `--agent-files <PATH>` replaces `--use-template`, with no comma and no `[repos].agent` lookup. The new name fits because the flag no longer copies a template tree.
- `--use-work-template`, `--use-agent-template`, `--use-agent-repo` and the root form aren't needed.
- A URL source can come after v0.3.1 if you still want it.

`--use-template ~/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1` would then just work, with the v0.3.0 caveat until v0.3.1 is released.

**Your two orders**
- **`cargo init` first:** this goes through the existing `--adopt`, which already keeps an adopted repo's `.gitignore`. I'd check it keeps the Rust `target/` entry.
- **`vc-x1 init` first:** `cargo init` then runs inside the dual repo. I haven't tested this, so I'd make both orders the rung's acceptance test.

**What being language-neutral exposes**
- **`validate` with no commands:** a fresh repo has no `[validate]` table, so `validate` should say plainly that it isn't configured yet. That also affects the close, land and push rungs.
- **`[closing] body`:** this one is neutral, so `init` should write it, which fixes the fresh-workspace close that needed `--body`.
- **The rules mention Rust:** 27 lines in `AGENTS.md` and `agent-data/` mention Rust or cargo, mostly in `code.md` and `versioning.md`. I haven't checked which are only examples, and that review belongs with v0.3.1 because those files are the proposal.
- **`vc-x1-template-2`:** it shrinks to just the rules. `CargoRust.toml`, the licenses, `version.toml` and the `agent/` payload go, and its first Todo, **Configure this workspace**, moves into the `TODO.md` that `init` writes.

I'd add this as a new rung right after **feat: init --test-repo makes a test repo**, so your test-repo work can commit as it stands.

The plain version: `init` gives any project in any language a dual repo with the rules and blank starter files, and never copies source or history. One path to the rules is all it needs, so the extra flags go away. A fresh repo has no validation commands until the project adds them, and `validate` should say so.

message.content:
Ideally I'd like to retire/delete vc-x1-template and base init on existing repos. To that end it'd be great if .vc-config was as repo neutral as possible. So we could add a global, maybe `base_name = vc-x1` and in vc-x1's .vc-config.md install would go from:
```
[install]
dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
commands = [
  "cp {profile.bin} {install.dir}/vc-x1{profile.suffix}.new",
  "mv {install.dir}/vc-x1{profile.suffix}.new {install.dir}/vc-x1{profile.suffix}",
]
```
to:
```
[install]
dir = "~/.cargo/bin"
commands = [
  "cp {profile.bin} {install.dir}/{base_name}{profile.suffix}.new",
  "mv {install.dir}/{base_name}{profile.suffix}.new {install.dir}/{base_name}{profile.suffix}",
]
```
 
thoughts?

content.text:
Yes to both, and they fit the rules: `AGENTS.md` already says there's no maintainer, only adopters. But one placeholder makes the config neutral only between Rust repos, so `init` needs a rule for what it takes from the base.

**The name key:** I'd use `[project] name = "vc-x1"` and `{project.name}`, not a global.
- **It avoids a TOML trap:** the config's blocks are concatenated, so a bare `base_name` outside the first block would land inside whichever table came before it.
- **It matches what's there:** placeholders are already `{table.key}`, and the schema documents keys that way.
- **It's separate from `family.member`:** that's the name siblings use and the messages record file. It can default to the project name.
- **Your example needs one more fill:** `[profile.*] bin = "target/release/vc-x1"` also holds the name, and `vc-x1` reads that value directly. Placeholders are filled only in command lists today, so this needs a small code change.

**What `init` does with each part of a base's config**

| Keys | Depends on | `init` |
|---|---|---|
| `[project]`, `[repos]`, `[remote]`, `[family] member` | the repo | writes its own |
| `[closing]`, `[record]`, `[test]` | nothing | copies |
| `[validate]`, `[build]`, `[install]`, `[profile.*]` | the language | copies only with a flag |

So a Python project based on `vc-x1` doesn't inherit `cargo clippy`, while `init --agent-files ~/.../vc-x1 --build-config` gives a new Rust repo a working setup. That also matches your "unless we add flags" condition.

`init` should write these keys out rather than copy the file. `.vc-config.md` also holds prose such as "wink's call 2026-10-21" and timing measurements, which belongs to `vc-x1`.

**What retiring the template costs**
- **Experiments spread:** an adopter's rules can hold unagreed experiments, and basing `init` on that repo copies them. Reading committed `main` keeps out unfinished rungs, but not experiments.

content.text:
You're right, and my "copies" row was wrong: none of those tables is universal. That makes the rule simpler: **`init` copies no config tables by default.**

**What `init` writes**
- **Always:** `[project]`, `[repos]`, and `[remote]` when needed.
- **On request:** the language tables, via `--build-config`, as before.
- **Your own setup:** `[family]`, `[record]` and `[test]` are never copied. Each project adds them when it wants them, and `custom.md`, which also isn't copied, is where you already adopt messaging.

**What happens when each key is missing**

| Key | Without it | Change needed |
|---|---|---|
| `[record]` | `commit --closing` moves nothing, as documented, and the record stays in `TODO.md`, as `AGENTS.md` says | none |
| `[family]` | no messaging; `agent-files diff` and `copy` need an explicit directory | none expected, worth confirming |
| `[closing] body` | `commit --closing` needs `--body`, the failure I hit on a fresh workspace | built-in default: `Closes the cycle "{title}".` |
| `[test] fixtures` | `src/test_helpers.rs` handles this case, but I haven't read what it does | check the behavior is sensible |

The closing default has to live in the code, because it can't mention `zCLOSED.md` in a repo that doesn't have one. `vc-x1` keeps its longer body in its own config. This also reverses what I said last time about `init` writing `[closing] body`.

**`.fixtures` to `tmp-durable`:** I think it's a good move, and fixtures are a clean match for your definition: reproducible, but you'd rather not lose them.
- **Why it's cheap:** the code reads the location from `[test] fixtures`, so only vc-x1's own files change: the config key (`tmp-durable/fixtures`), `.gitignore`, `README.md`, and the fixture build command.
- **Why it's cleaner:** a project-specific top-level directory goes away, and `.fixtures` stays out of what `init` generates.
- **Timing:** it isn't tied to v0.3.1, so I'd file it as a small Todo.

**`tmp-durable` needs one thing to be portable:** v0.3.1's scratch rule names `tmp/` and `tmp-durable/`, but the only `tmp-durable` hits in `src/` are the `--test-repo` tests, so `init` doesn't write it. The `.gitignore` that `init` generates should list it, or a fresh repo could commit what's in there. It's worth checking `tmp/` at the same time. That belongs in the `init` rung.

The plain version: `init` writes only the repo's name and layout, and your family, messages, record files and fixtures stay your own setup. The missing-key cases should mostly work already, except that `commit --closing` needs a built-in default body. Moving fixtures to `tmp-durable` is a good small change for later, and `init` should ignore that directory in new repos.

content.text:
I'd use commands, with one small addition, and put them in your own config instead of a table in each repo. "For my repos, always" describes you, not any one base repo, and `~/.config/vc-x1/config.toml` already exists and is already loaded when `init` runs.

**Why the user config**
- **Safety:** if a base repo's config could list commands, then `init` from someone's repo, or later from a URL, would run whatever they wrote. Your own file only runs what you put there.
- **Scope:** `init` stays neutral for everyone else, as you wanted, and only you get your setup.

**Why commands over a file list**
- **A list falls short:** it could copy `custom.md`, but it couldn't create a messages record or do any other setup step.
- **The pattern exists:** `[validate]`, `[build]` and `[install]` are already command lists, and `src/command_list.rs` already fills and runs them.

**The addition:** `[family]`, `[record]` and `[closing]` are tables inside `.vc-config.md`, not files, so a copy command can't add them. Each list element also looks like a single invocation, not a shell line, so `cat >> .vc-config.md` wouldn't work without `sh -c`. A fragment file is cleaner:

```toml
[init]
config = "~/.config/vc-x1/my-repos.md"   # tables added to each new .vc-config.md
commands = [
  "cp {init.base}/custom.md custom.md",
]
```

The fragment can use `{project.name}`, so it can set `member = "{project.name}"`, and `{init.base}` is the path given to `--agent-files`.

**Details to settle**
- **Order:** these run after `init` writes its files and before its first commit, so the results land in that commit.
- **Failure:** a failed command stops `init` before anything is pushed, and it prints what it left behind.
- **Testing:** this needs a `--no-user-init` flag, otherwise your own test repos would always get your setup and you couldn't see what another adopter gets.
- **Relative paths:** `family.messages = "../vc-x1-messages"` resolves against the new repo, so it breaks for a repo in `~/tmp`. The fragment would need to use an absolute path, and that key's value would have to allow `~`.

**Timing:** I'd file this as a Todo after v0.3.1. It's a convenience, and until it exists you can add your setup by hand after `init`. Nothing in this cycle's `init` rung blocks it.

The plain version: your personal config gets a list of commands to run and a file of settings to add for every new repo, so `init` stays neutral for everyone else. Keeping it there also means a repo you base on can't make your machine run anything. It can wait until after v0.3.1.

content.text:
I'd build the inverted form first, even though you lean toward `[init]`. Nothing has changed in the repo, and the rung is still held uncommitted.

**The inverted form:** your own script wraps a neutral `vc-x1`:

```sh
vc-x1 init "$1" --agent-files ~/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1 --no-push
cd "$1"
cp ~/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1/custom.md .
cat ~/.config/vc-x1/my-repos.md >> .vc-config.md    # the tables
vc-x1 commit -s w --title "chore: my repo setup" --body "..."
# then push both repos
```

| | `[init]` in the config | Script around `vc-x1` |
|---|---|---|
| New in `vc-x1` | config keys, placeholders, command running, `--no-user-init`, failure reporting | `init --no-push`, which it doesn't have today |
| Neutrality | neutral only because you configure it separately | complete, since `vc-x1` knows nothing about your setup |
| Testing what another adopter gets | needs a flag | just run `vc-x1 init` |
| Safety | needs the rule that only the user config can run commands | no issue, since it's your script |
| History | your setup is mixed into the first commit | separate commit, so generic and personal stay distinct |
| Typing and discovery | better: plain `init` does everything | you have to remember to run your script |
| Target forms | `init` has already worked out the path | the script has to handle them, or take just one form |

**Why the script first**
- **It matches this cycle:** close, land and push became separate steps you can put testing between. `init`, your setup, then push is the same idea.
- **It's easy to undo:** `init --no-push` is useful either way, while `[init]` keys become a schema to maintain.
- **It keeps the option open:** if the script gets clumsy, `[init]` can still be added, and it would mostly just run that same script. You'd also know by then what it really needs.

**The costs**
- **`--no-push` needs care:** `init` currently pushes as part of creating each repo, including updating the agent-repo with its final IDs. Separating that is a real change, not just a flag check, and I haven't sized it. A failed script would leave the repos local and unpushed, which is at least easy to recover from.
- **A missing piece:** the script still has to push the first time, including the bookmark setup `init` does today. That may mean a new `vc-x1` step.
- **What would change my mind:** if splitting the push turns out to be large, `[init]` becomes the cheaper option, because it runs before the first commit and leaves pushing alone.

**Order:** size the `--no-push` split first, and let that settle the choice. It doesn't block v0.3.1, because until either exists you can add your setup by hand after `init`, so I'd file this as a Todo after the release.

The plain version: keep `vc-x1` knowing nothing about your setup, and put your extra copying in your own script, which needs `init` to be able to stop before pushing. Your `[init]` table remains the fallback if making `init` stop there turns out to be hard, and neither has to happen before v0.3.1.

content.text:
You didn't miss anything. `init` pushes, then your script commits on top and pushes again, and that's an ordinary fast-forward, not a rewrite. I was wrong that it needs `--no-push`, and wrong that the script would need to handle the first push.

That removes the main cost I listed for the script, so it now needs nothing new in `vc-x1` beyond what's already planned for this cycle: `--agent-files` and `[project] name`. The flow is:

```sh
vc-x1 init "$1" --agent-files ~/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1
cd "$1"
cp ~/data/prgs/rust/vc-x1/custom.md .
cat ~/.config/vc-x1/my-repos.md >> .vc-config.md
vc-x1 commit -s w --title "chore: my repo setup" --body "..."
```

For `--test-repo` it's the same, except `commit` pushes to the local remotes beside the test repo.

**What's left**
- **A small window:** the remote has the neutral repo without your setup for the seconds between the two pushes. That doesn't matter.
- **Editing the config:** `cat >>` works because the config's blocks are concatenated, but a fragment that repeats a table `init` already wrote would break the TOML. `vc-x1 validate-config` after the `cat` would catch that.

So I'd go with the script, keep `[init]` as an idea in case the script ever grows awkward, and file nothing for `vc-x1` beyond this cycle's `init` rung.

The plain version: you're right. `init` pushes a neutral repo, your script adds your files and commits again, and that needs no changes to `vc-x1` beyond what this cycle already plans.

What is being done: the running cycle's planning and its work's documentation. The last
finished cycle's is in [zCLOSED.md](zCLOSED.md), and what we might do is in [TODO.md](TODO.md). The
block's shape is on trial: it opens with the Todo as it was picked from `TODO.md`, then the
Deliberation, the plan, Solution and Acceptance check, and the Ladder with its details.

This file is a trial (2026-10-09). The agent-files still name `TODO.md > ## In Progress` as the
record's home, and the cycle that makes this file the rule is [The cycle-record moves out of
TODO.md into zDOING.md](TODO.md#the-cycle-record-moves-out-of-todomd-into-zdoingmd).

**Rule:** a cycle changing `vc-x1` runs its own latest build, wink's (2026-10-30): `vc-x1-dev`,
installed after the rung before, for every command, `validate` and `install` as well as `commit`. The
landed `vc-x1` is used only for a sequence `vc-x1-dev` cannot run, and saying so. Until **install has a role and a
profile** runs, `vc-x1-dev install` needs `--profile dev`, since bare it builds and replaces the landed
`vc-x1`.

## Continuation notes

Where the agent was, for the agent that comes next. Ephemeral, never a record: read first, acted
on, and reset to `_None._` by the reader. Kept here by the trial and no longer in `TODO.md`,
where [Acquaint](AGENTS.md#acquaint) still says to look.

Kept at the acquaint of 2026-11-02:

- **chore: carry setting a mistake aside into v0.3.1** was set aside when **WIP: cleanup** was
  dropped and is not done, and its files, `tmp/mistake-aside-todo.patch` and
  `tmp/mistake-aside-zDOING.md`, are gone from `tmp/`. Session
  `520a2a50-1afc-4282-a824-bc78c27b7cc5` in the agent-repo is where they were made. The edits:
  **Setting a mistake aside** added to **agent-files(proposal): v0.3.1**, **abandon and revert set a
  mistake aside** deleted from `## Todo`, and a reread note on **squash-push shows what it takes,
  and push follows jj**.
- `wflow.sh`, `wflow2.sh`, and `wflow3.sh` are the trials behind the matrix in **commit works at every
  scope, and --local keeps it on the machine**. They are gone from `tmp/`, and each `Write` of them is in
  that session's transcript, the last at lines 698, 716, and 742.

Left at the end of 2026-11-02:

- The rung **feat: init --test-repo makes a test repo** is `(current)` and uncommitted, held while
  wink tests. Tests t2 and t3 in `~/tmp` passed with `--use-template` taking a root and expanding
  `~` after the comma. On wink's go: a full `vc-x1-dev validate`, since it may not have run after
  the last edit, then flip, describe, `vc-x1-dev commit -s w --no-push`, and install dev.
- The next rung, agreed in thoughts and not yet in the ladder: `init` initializes a dual repo for
  any language and never duplicates one.
  - `--agent-files <PATH>` replaces `--use-template`, and the comma form, the root form, and the
    `<work>.claude` default go. The path may be a working repo such as `vc-x1`, and only its
    committed agent-files are copied, the set `vc-x1 agent-files copy` copies. Never `TODO.md`,
    source, or transcripts.
  - `init` writes the neutral starting files itself, a blank `TODO.md` and `CLAUDE.md`, and a
    `.gitignore` that lists `tmp-durable` (check `tmp` too).
  - `[project] name` and a `{project.name}` placeholder, filled in `[profile.*] bin` as well as in
    command lists, so `vc-x1`'s `[install]` names no project. A table, not a top-level key, since
    the config's blocks are concatenated.
  - `init` writes `[project]`, `[repos]`, and `[remote]` only. The language tables (`[validate]`,
    `[build]`, `[install]`, `[profile.*]`) copy only on a flag, its name unsettled. `[family]`,
    `[record]`, `[test]`, and `[closing]` are never copied, being wink's own setup.
  - `commit --closing` gets a built-in default body, `Closes the cycle "{title}".`, for a config
    with no `[closing] body`.
  - Unchecked: what `src/test_helpers.rs` does with no `[test] fixtures`, and `agent-files diff`
    and `copy` with no `[family]`.
- wink's own setup is a script around a neutral `vc-x1`: `init`, copy `custom.md`, append a config
  fragment, `vc-x1 validate-config`, then `vc-x1 commit`. It needs no `--no-push` (wink's
  correction), since the commit fast-forwards what `init` pushed. An `[init]` table in the user
  config stays only an idea, for if the script grows awkward.
- Todos to file, all after v0.3.1: retire `vc-x1-template` and base `init` on existing repos (a
  rule change to Terminology, **Changing the agent-files**, and `family.template`, and its deletion
  is wink's go after checking which siblings name it); `.fixtures` moves to `tmp-durable/fixtures`;
  URL sources for `--agent-files`. For the v0.3.1 proposal itself: the 27 lines of the agent-files
  naming Rust or cargo get a read for which are only examples. `vc-x1-template-2` shrinks to the
  rules once the next rung lands.
